extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and others interested in publication integrity and peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for detecting, investigating, responding to, and preventing fabricated or manipulated peer review in scholarly publishing. Covers publisher investigative steps, reporting, remediation (retraction/resubmission), and preventive editorial practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect fake reviewer email addresses via editorial checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial checks spotted fake email addresses, prompting further investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should actively screen reviewer contact information (e.g., check that suggested reviewer emails are legitimate and not contrived) as an initial detection measure. In this case, identification of fake email addresses triggered a deeper inquiry into peer-review integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct internal investigations to uncover fabricated peer review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent internal investigations uncovered fabricated peer review reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When anomalies are detected, publishers must perform thorough internal investigations to determine whether peer review reports were fabricated, who was responsible, and the scope of the compromise before deciding on corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retract articles when the peer review process is found to be compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: Springer confirms that 64 articles are being retracted ... after a thorough investigation we have strong reason to believe that the peer review process on these 64 articles was compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If investigation shows the peer-review process was compromised and reports cannot be trusted, retraction is an appropriate corrective action to protect the integrity of the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report manipulation findings to COPE and follow COPE recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: We reported this to the Committee on Publishing Ethics (COPE) immediately ... and has followed COPE’s recommendations, as outlined in their statement, for dealing with this issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should notify relevant oversight bodies (e.g., COPE) about systematic manipulation and adopt established recommendations and best practices for remediation and prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspond with affected corresponding authors and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher is ... corresponding with the individual authors and institutions affected by the retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should communicate transparently and directly with corresponding authors and their institutions during investigations and after decisions, both to inform and to assist institutional inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage resubmission and legitimate peer review where authors are cleared
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations where institutional investigations have found that authors have been inadvertently affected by the compromised peer review process, they will be encouraged to resubmit and go through a legitimate peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors are found not culpable, offer a pathway to republish by subjecting the work to proper independent peer review, rather than permanently penalizing uninvolved authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and strengthen editorial processes across the publisher to guard against manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: We are now reviewing our editorial processes across Springer to guard against this kind of manipulation of the peer review process in future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should audit and revise editorial workflows, update policies, and implement systematic safeguards to reduce vulnerability to reviewer-identity manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase credential checks for suggested peer reviewers (institutional email, Scopus ID)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credentials from peer reviewers will be increasingly checked by our editorial office ... and some journals may request more information in the form of an institutional e-mail address and/or SCOPUS ID of the suggested reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require verifiable identifiers (institutional emails, ORCID/Scopus IDs) for suggested reviewers and have editorial staff validate those credentials before inviting reviewers. This reduces risk from fabricated reviewer identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and educate external editors to ensure thorough reviewer vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: We are working to support our external editors to make them aware of the issues and ensure that thorough checks of peer reviewers are completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide training, clear procedures, and operational support for external editors so they perform consistent and robust checks on reviewer identities and qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate involvement of third-party agencies and other intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings suggest some third party agencies, offering pre-submission editing and submission assistance services to authors, may have been involved during the submission process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should consider whether external agencies or intermediaries participated in or enabled manipulation; policies may be needed regarding disclosure or limits on third-party submission assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume author culpability without institutional investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors are not always to blame for faked emails. Recently, BMC cleared the authors of a retracted paper of responsibility ... In the 64 papers retracted today, too, the authors may not always have been involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should avoid presuming author misconduct solely because reviews were fabricated; coordinate with institutions to determine responsibility before assigning blame or taking author-level sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider transparent publication of which articles were retracted and why
rubrics_metrics.description: We’re still not sure which papers have been retracted, but will keep checking the Springer site for new notices and will update the post when we know more. [Update ... Here are the 64 papers.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make retraction notices specific and publicly accessible (listing affected articles and clear reasons) so readers and citing authors can identify and respond to retractions promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor large bibliographies for retractions (practical tool recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion in comments: write a small Python script that takes in a DOI, downloads the webpage for that paper, gets the appropriate part of the HTML and hashes it (MD5) ... then alerts you to all cases where the hashes don’t match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers managing large reference lists should adopt systematic monitoring (automated checking of DOIs/webpages or use of services/databases tracking retractions) to detect when cited items are retracted or altered.
